# Workspace Copilot An AI-assistant showcase inspired by Copilot-class plugins. It inspects the active repository through a lifecycle-scoped Node backend, identifies languages, frameworks, scripts, and important files, then opens a Composer-adjacent suggestion popover that inserts grounded intents directly into the active draft. Public contracts demonstrated: - `weworkPluginRuntime` - `ctx.wework.backend` - `ctx.wework.chat.providers` - `ctx.wework.commands` - `ctx.wework.composer` - `composer.slash` - `wework.composer.action` The scanner uses breadth-first sampling so a large first package cannot consume the whole scan budget and hide the rest of a monorepo. # Wegent > An open-source work system where people and AI move projects forward together. English | [简体中文](README_zh.md) [![CI](https://github.com/wecode-ai/Wegent/actions/workflows/test.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/wecode-ai/Wegent/actions/workflows/test.yml) [![License](https://img.shields.io/github/license/wecode-ai/Wegent)](LICENSE) [![GitHub Issues](https://img.shields.io/github/issues/wecode-ai/Wegent)](https://github.com/wecode-ai/Wegent/issues) Wegent brings team members, AI agents, and personal stand-ins together around the same Issue: describe a goal, assign work, execute tasks, and deliver results. Discussions, execution records, and deliverables stay connected. Work on a local coding project on your own, or hand work across your team in a shared project space. [Download the latest Wegent Desktop](https://github.com/wecode-ai/Wegent/releases/latest) · [Quick start](#quick-start) · [Documentation](https://wecode-ai.github.io/wegent-docs/) · [Contributing](CONTRIBUTING.md) ## One Issue, the whole team [![Watch the 90-second collaboration demo (English)](https://github.com/wecode-ai/Wegent/releases/download/readme-assets/wegent-ai-collaboration-en-20261109.jpg)](https://github.com/wecode-ai/Wegent/releases/download/readme-assets/wegent-ai-collaboration-en-20261109.mp4) [Watch the full demo (90 seconds, English)](https://github.com/wecode-ai/Wegent/releases/download/readme-assets/wegent-ai-collaboration-en-20261109.mp4) Start with “Build an interactive three-column iteration board.” Here is how the work can move forward: 1. **Describe the goal** — Create an Issue and choose a team member, agent, or collaboration group to handle it. 2. **Assign the work** — A configured AI lead can delegate planning and implementation to the appropriate roles. Members receive notifications and open the same Issue. 3. **Execute and deliver** — Members create linked tasks in Wework, use AI to work with files, commands, and tests, then select results to deliver back to the Issue. 4. **Discuss and hand off** — Add feedback and reassign from the discussion. The next member or agent continues with the existing plan and files. 5. **Let a stand-in help, then confirm** — A configured personal stand-in handles work according to its intake scope and processing policy, then hands it back for your confirmation. **Assignment is not completion, and AI output is not personal confirmation.** The Issue connects ownership, execution, discussion, and deliverables so the team can inspect progress, ask questions, and continue the work.

Organize work in a project space with task boards, shared files, and execution status.

## Core capabilities - **People and AI working together** — Assign, discuss, and hand off Issues among team members, agents, and collaboration groups in one project. - **Task execution and delivery** — Create linked tasks from Issues, inspect execution, and deliver selected files and notes back to the project. - **Personal stand-ins (Beta)** — Receive work from authorized project sources according to configured responsibilities and processing policies, with execution records and human-intervention controls. - **Project management and automation** — Organize projects with task boards, shared files, execution records, and deliverables. Configure automatic processing rules and execution queues. - **Local coding workbench** — Use Codex directly with project code, files, commands, and development environments. Review tool activity, tests, and diffs together. - **Reusable agents and execution targets** — Combine models, prompts, Skills, knowledge, and tools. Run tasks locally, on remote work machines, or with server-managed executors. - **Self-hosting** — Deploy Wegent Web and Backend so your team can manage access, permissions, models, scheduling, knowledge services, and remote devices. Personal stand-ins require source authorization, model configuration, and an available execution device. Automatic processing follows project permissions and operation approvals; it does not mean work continues on a powered-off computer. See the [project lead guide](docs/en/wework/personal-stand-in.md#project-lead-controls) for AI lead conversation and automatic-processing requirements; lead conversations currently require experimental features to be enabled. See [Personal stand-in and scenario roles](docs/en/wework/personal-stand-in.md) for configuration. ## Quick start ### Personal use: complete a task in a local project 1. [Download the latest Wegent Desktop installer](https://github.com/wecode-ai/Wegent/releases/latest) and install it. 2. Open the app, follow model setup, and add or select a local project. Local work does not require Wegent Backend login. 3. Create a task describing what to analyze, change, or verify. 4. Inspect agent activity, command output, test results, and file diffs to review the outcome. ### Team collaboration: start with one Issue 1. Create a collaboration project. For shared team access, connect to Wegent Backend and create or join a cloud collaboration project. 2. Add project members. For AI execution, explicitly add agents and configure an available execution environment and model. 3. Create an Issue, describe its goal, and assign it to a member, agent, or collaboration group. 4. Create a linked task from the Issue and deliver the results after execution. Use comments to give feedback and hand work to the next owner. 5. To let a personal stand-in help, configure its project sources, responsibilities, and processing policy in **My stand-in**, then handle human questions and confirmations as needed. New projects do not automatically add agents or enable stand-ins. See [Creating Issues in Collaboration](docs/en/wegent/user-guide/coding/collaboration-issue-home.md) and the [personal stand-in guide](docs/en/wework/personal-stand-in.md) for detailed controls. ### Self-host Wegent Web and Backend To start the self-hosted web application and Backend in standalone mode with Docker: ```bash curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/wecode-ai/Wegent/main/install.sh | bash -s -- --standalone ``` Open http://localhost:3000 and follow the setup flow to create the administrator password and configure a model. See the [Installation Guide](docs/en/wegent/getting-started/installation.md) and [Standalone Mode](docs/en/wegent/deployment/standalone-mode.md) for other deployment options. ## Products ### Wework / Wegent Desktop Wework is the Wegent desktop workbench, connecting project collaboration to execution. It retains the full local coding workflow: organize conversations by project and task, work directly with files, run commands and tests, and review changes and diffs in one workbench. Connect to Backend to use shared project spaces, cloud models, and remote execution devices.

Running and reviewing a local coding task in Wegent Desktop.

### Wegent Web and Backend Wegent Web provides browser-based project collaboration, remote agents, knowledge, automation, and administration. Agents use configured models, knowledge, Skills, and tools. Backend provides shared project resources, access permissions, APIs, scheduling, and execution-device management. Teams can self-host Web and Backend to manage their services and data.

A Wegent remote agent uses tools to generate a Gantt chart.

## Development Requires Node.js 22.15+ (22.x) or 23.8+ (Node.js 24 recommended), and pnpm: ```bash pnpm install pnpm --filter wework dev ``` To run the macOS desktop app: ```bash pnpm --filter wework dev:mac ``` See [wework/README.md](wework/README.md) for desktop development, build, and release instructions. `wework/` is the current desktop application source directory. In the desktop architecture, Electron provides system capabilities and process management, DeepSeek Harness (DSH) hosts the product UI and plugins, and Executor manages tasks and sessions while driving Codex execution. See the [DSH application host](wework/dsh/app-wework/README.en.md) for plugin extension points and [Cloud project collaboration architecture](docs/en/wegent/developer-guide/cloud-project-collaboration.md) for shared-resource and execution boundaries. ## Repository map ### Products and services | Directory | Responsibility | | -------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------- | | `wework/` | Wegent Desktop (Electron, Vite, React) | | `wework-mobile/` | Independent Expo application for iOS and Android | | `frontend/` | Wegent Web (Next.js, React) | | `backend/` | Default public API, business logic, and data models | | `backend-rs/` | Rust hybrid gateway and APIs that have completed migration | | `executor/` | Rust task executor, local-device runtime, and Codex integration | | `executor_manager/` | Server-side executor scheduling, sandboxes, and orchestration | | `chat_shell/` | Lightweight chat and agent runtime | | `knowledge_runtime/` | Knowledge indexing and retrieval API | | `knowledge_doc_converter/` | Document parsing and asynchronous conversion service | ### Shared code and developer tools | Directory | Responsibility | | ------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | `knowledge_engine/` | Reusable Python kernel for parsing, indexing, vector stores, and retrieval | | `shared/` | Python models, protocols, utilities, and telemetry shared by services | | `packages/` | TypeScript chat and collaboration modules shared by Web and Desktop | | `sdk/` | Plugin authentication, build, creation, and DingTalk workspace SDKs | | `wegent-cli/` | Python CLI for managing Wegent CRD resources | ### Infrastructure, tests, and documentation | Directory | Responsibility | | ----------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | `docker/` | Service images, standalone resources, and the `docker/telemetry/` observability stack | | `scripts/` | Installation, release, acceptance, repository-policy, and development automation | | `tests/` | Cross-service Playwright integration tests and installation tests | | `docs/` | English and Chinese user docs, developer docs, architecture, and historical designs | | `patches/` | Third-party dependency patches used by pnpm `patchedDependencies` | | `LICENSES/` | Third-party license texts required for repository distribution | | `.github/` | CI, release workflows, composite actions, and repository automation | ### Root entry points | File | Responsibility | | -------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------- | | `start.sh`, `install.sh` | Local startup and self-hosted installation | | `build_image.sh`, `build_image_mac.sh` | Multi-architecture and host Docker image builds | | `docker-compose*.yml` | Default, build, and E2E Compose orchestration | | `package.json`, `pnpm-workspace.yaml` | JavaScript/TypeScript workspace definition | | `pyproject.toml`, `uv.lock` | Repository-level Python tooling and lock metadata | | `AGENTS.md`, `CLAUDE.md` | Contributor rules and compatibility symlink | ## Documentation - [Wegent Desktop documentation](docs/en/wework/README.md) - [Desktop development and release](wework/README.md) - [Wegent quick start](docs/en/wegent/getting-started/quick-start.md) - [Installation and deployment](docs/en/wegent/getting-started/installation.md) - [Core concepts](docs/en/wegent/concepts/core-concepts.md) - [Developer guide](docs/en/wegent/developer-guide/README.md) - [Troubleshooting](docs/en/wegent/troubleshooting.md) ## Contributing Bug reports, documentation improvements, code contributions, and new ways of using Wegent are all welcome. - [Contributing Guide](CONTRIBUTING.md) - [Security Policy](SECURITY.md) - [GitHub Issues](https://github.com/wecode-ai/Wegent/issues) - DingTalk Community: “wework社区交流”, group ID `190890002451` - [Discord Community](https://discord.gg/MVzJzyqEUp) - [License](LICENSE) ## # Wework DSH 扩展 Demo 这是“Wework 插件开发”Skill 携带的可运行 Core DSH 插件示例，覆盖 Wework 当前公开的全部 UI 扩展点。模型可以复制该目录作为实现参考；桌面应用不会自动启用 它。 先把该目录复制到可写的项目目录，再在 Wework 的“插件 → 管理 → Wework 插件”中 输入复制后目录的绝对路径，例如： ```text file:/absolute/path/to/ui-extension-demo ``` 安装完成后重启 Core DSH。左侧会出现 `DSH Demo`，应用切换器、设置页、Composer、 工作区工具栏、底部面板、新建工作区 Tab 菜单和全局 overlay 也会出现对应示例。 示例还注册了一个可从 Composer、工作区工具栏以及 `Command+Shift+D` （Windows/Linux 为 `Ctrl+Shift+D`）触发的统一命令，并演示上下文条件、配置和 持久化状态。 停用或卸载插件并重启后，所有贡献会随同一 DSH 生命周期一起移除。 关键文件： - `package.json` 声明 DSH bundle、client 依赖和浏览器平台。 - `cordis.patch.yml` 把插件加入 DSH Loader 树。 - `index.js` 是 host 入口；纯 UI 插件可以保持为空。 - `client.js` 通过 `ctx.wework` 注册命令、菜单、快捷键、配置与状态，并通过 `ctx.wework.contributions` 注册宿主描述、通过原生 `ctx.slots.register` 注册自定义 UI。 - 左侧 `DSH Demo` 入口通过公开的 `workspaceTab` 路由参数首次创建独立 Tab， 后续点击复用同一个 Tab，不会覆盖用户当前正在使用的 Tab。 生产插件应更换包名、ID、文案和样式，并只注册实际需要的扩展点。 # Wegent > An open-source work system where people and AI move projects forward together. English | [简体中文](README_zh.md) [![CI](https://github.com/wecode-ai/Wegent/actions/workflows/test.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/wecode-ai/Wegent/actions/workflows/test.yml) [![License](https://img.shields.io/github/license/wecode-ai/Wegent)](LICENSE) [![GitHub Issues](https://img.shields.io/github/issues/wecode-ai/Wegent)](https://github.com/wecode-ai/Wegent/issues) Wegent brings team members, AI agents, and personal stand-ins together around the same Issue: describe a goal, assign work, execute tasks, and deliver results. Discussions, execution records, and deliverables stay connected. Work on a local coding project on your own, or hand work across your team in a shared project space. [Download the latest Wegent Desktop](https://github.com/wecode-ai/Wegent/releases/latest) · [Quick start](#quick-start) · [Documentation](https://wecode-ai.github.io/wegent-docs/) · [Contributing](CONTRIBUTING.md) ## One Issue, the whole team [![Watch the 90-second collaboration demo (English)](https://github.com/wecode-ai/Wegent/releases/download/readme-assets/wegent-ai-collaboration-en-20261109.jpg)](https://github.com/wecode-ai/Wegent/releases/download/readme-assets/wegent-ai-collaboration-en-20261109.mp4) [Watch the full demo (90 seconds, English)](https://github.com/wecode-ai/Wegent/releases/download/readme-assets/wegent-ai-collaboration-en-20261109.mp4) Start with “Build an interactive three-column iteration board.” Here is how the work can move forward: 1. **Describe the goal** — Create an Issue and choose a team member, agent, or collaboration group to handle it. 2. **Assign the work** — A configured AI lead can delegate planning and implementation to the appropriate roles. Members receive notifications and open the same Issue. 3. **Execute and deliver** — Members create linked tasks in Wework, use AI to work with files, commands, and tests, then select results to deliver back to the Issue. 4. **Discuss and hand off** — Add feedback and reassign from the discussion. The next member or agent continues with the existing plan and files. 5. **Let a stand-in help, then confirm** — A configured personal stand-in handles work according to its intake scope and processing policy, then hands it back for your confirmation. **Assignment is not completion, and AI output is not personal confirmation.** The Issue connects ownership, execution, discussion, and deliverables so the team can inspect progress, ask questions, and continue the work.

Organize work in a project space with task boards, shared files, and execution status.

## Core capabilities - **People and AI working together** — Assign, discuss, and hand off Issues among team members, agents, and collaboration groups in one project. - **Task execution and delivery** — Create linked tasks from Issues, inspect execution, and deliver selected files and notes back to the project. - **Personal stand-ins (Beta)** — Receive work from authorized project sources according to configured responsibilities and processing policies, with execution records and human-intervention controls. - **Project management and automation** — Organize projects with task boards, shared files, execution records, and deliverables. Configure automatic processing rules and execution queues. - **Local coding workbench** — Use Codex directly with project code, files, commands, and development environments. Review tool activity, tests, and diffs together. - **Reusable agents and execution targets** — Combine models, prompts, Skills, knowledge, and tools. Run tasks locally, on remote work machines, or with server-managed executors. - **Self-hosting** — Deploy Wegent Web and Backend so your team can manage access, permissions, models, scheduling, knowledge services, and remote devices. Personal stand-ins require source authorization, model configuration, and an available execution device. Automatic processing follows project permissions and operation approvals; it does not mean work continues on a powered-off computer. See the [project lead guide](docs/en/wework/personal-stand-in.md#project-lead-controls) for AI lead conversation and automatic-processing requirements; lead conversations currently require experimental features to be enabled. See [Personal stand-in and scenario roles](docs/en/wework/personal-stand-in.md) for configuration. ## Quick start ### Personal use: complete a task in a local project 1. [Download the latest Wegent Desktop installer](https://github.com/wecode-ai/Wegent/releases/latest) and install it. 2. Open the app, follow model setup, and add or select a local project. Local work does not require Wegent Backend login. 3. Create a task describing what to analyze, change, or verify. 4. Inspect agent activity, command output, test results, and file diffs to review the outcome. ### Team collaboration: start with one Issue 1. Create a collaboration project. For shared team access, connect to Wegent Backend and create or join a cloud collaboration project. 2. Add project members. For AI execution, explicitly add agents and configure an available execution environment and model. 3. Create an Issue, describe its goal, and assign it to a member, agent, or collaboration group. 4. Create a linked task from the Issue and deliver the results after execution. Use comments to give feedback and hand work to the next owner. 5. To let a personal stand-in help, configure its project sources, responsibilities, and processing policy in **My stand-in**, then handle human questions and confirmations as needed. New projects do not automatically add agents or enable stand-ins. See [Creating Issues in Collaboration](docs/en/wegent/user-guide/coding/collaboration-issue-home.md) and the [personal stand-in guide](docs/en/wework/personal-stand-in.md) for detailed controls. ### Self-host Wegent Web and Backend To start the self-hosted web application and Backend in standalone mode with Docker: ```bash curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/wecode-ai/Wegent/main/install.sh | bash -s -- --standalone ``` Open http://localhost:3000 and follow the setup flow to create the administrator password and configure a model. See the [Installation Guide](docs/en/wegent/getting-started/installation.md) and [Standalone Mode](docs/en/wegent/deployment/standalone-mode.md) for other deployment options. ## Products ### Wework / Wegent Desktop Wework is the Wegent desktop workbench, connecting project collaboration to execution. It retains the full local coding workflow: organize conversations by project and task, work directly with files, run commands and tests, and review changes and diffs in one workbench. Connect to Backend to use shared project spaces, cloud models, and remote execution devices.

Running and reviewing a local coding task in Wegent Desktop.

### Wegent Web and Backend Wegent Web provides browser-based project collaboration, remote agents, knowledge, automation, and administration. Agents use configured models, knowledge, Skills, and tools. Backend provides shared project resources, access permissions, APIs, scheduling, and execution-device management. Teams can self-host Web and Backend to manage their services and data.

A Wegent remote agent uses tools to generate a Gantt chart.

## Development Requires Node.js 22.15+ (22.x) or 23.8+ (Node.js 24 recommended), and pnpm: ```bash pnpm install pnpm --filter wework dev ``` To run the macOS desktop app: ```bash pnpm --filter wework dev:mac ``` See [wework/README.md](wework/README.md) for desktop development, build, and release instructions. `wework/` is the current desktop application source directory. In the desktop architecture, Electron provides system capabilities and process management, DeepSeek Harness (DSH) hosts the product UI and plugins, and Executor manages tasks and sessions while driving Codex execution. See the [DSH application host](wework/dsh/app-wework/README.en.md) for plugin extension points and [Cloud project collaboration architecture](docs/en/wegent/developer-guide/cloud-project-collaboration.md) for shared-resource and execution boundaries. ## Repository map ### Products and services | Directory | Responsibility | | -------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------- | | `wework/` | Wegent Desktop (Electron, Vite, React) | | `wework-mobile/` | Independent Expo application for iOS and Android | | `frontend/` | Wegent Web (Next.js, React) | | `backend/` | Default public API, business logic, and data models | | `backend-rs/` | Rust hybrid gateway and APIs that have completed migration | | `executor/` | Rust task executor, local-device runtime, and Codex integration | | `executor_manager/` | Server-side executor scheduling, sandboxes, and orchestration | | `chat_shell/` | Lightweight chat and agent runtime | | `knowledge_runtime/` | Knowledge indexing and retrieval API | | `knowledge_doc_converter/` | Document parsing and asynchronous conversion service | ### Shared code and developer tools | Directory | Responsibility | | ------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | `knowledge_engine/` | Reusable Python kernel for parsing, indexing, vector stores, and retrieval | | `shared/` | Python models, protocols, utilities, and telemetry shared by services | | `packages/` | TypeScript chat and collaboration modules shared by Web and Desktop | | `sdk/` | Plugin authentication, build, creation, and DingTalk workspace SDKs | | `wegent-cli/` | Python CLI for managing Wegent CRD resources | ### Infrastructure, tests, and documentation | Directory | Responsibility | | ----------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | `docker/` | Service images, standalone resources, and the `docker/telemetry/` observability stack | | `scripts/` | Installation, release, acceptance, repository-policy, and development automation | | `tests/` | Cross-service Playwright integration tests and installation tests | | `docs/` | English and Chinese user docs, developer docs, architecture, and historical designs | | `patches/` | Third-party dependency patches used by pnpm `patchedDependencies` | | `LICENSES/` | Third-party license texts required for repository distribution | | `.github/` | CI, release workflows, composite actions, and repository automation | ### Root entry points | File | Responsibility | | -------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------- | | `start.sh`, `install.sh` | Local startup and self-hosted installation | | `build_image.sh`, `build_image_mac.sh` | Multi-architecture and host Docker image builds | | `docker-compose*.yml` | Default, build, and E2E Compose orchestration | | `package.json`, `pnpm-workspace.yaml` | JavaScript/TypeScript workspace definition | | `pyproject.toml`, `uv.lock` | Repository-level Python tooling and lock metadata | | `AGENTS.md`, `CLAUDE.md` | Contributor rules and compatibility symlink | ## Documentation - [Wegent Desktop documentation](docs/en/wework/README.md) - [Desktop development and release](wework/README.md) - [Wegent quick start](docs/en/wegent/getting-started/quick-start.md) - [Installation and deployment](docs/en/wegent/getting-started/installation.md) - [Core concepts](docs/en/wegent/concepts/core-concepts.md) - [Developer guide](docs/en/wegent/developer-guide/README.md) - [Troubleshooting](docs/en/wegent/troubleshooting.md) ## Contributing Bug reports, documentation improvements, code contributions, and new ways of using Wegent are all welcome. - [Contributing Guide](CONTRIBUTING.md) - [Security Policy](SECURITY.md) - [GitHub Issues](https://github.com/wecode-ai/Wegent/issues) - DingTalk Community: “wework社区交流”, group ID `190890002451` - [Discord Community](https://discord.gg/MVzJzyqEUp) - [License](LICENSE) ## # Wegent > An open-source work system where people and AI move projects forward together. English | [简体中文](README_zh.md) [![CI](https://github.com/wecode-ai/Wegent/actions/workflows/test.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/wecode-ai/Wegent/actions/workflows/test.yml) [![License](https://img.shields.io/github/license/wecode-ai/Wegent)](LICENSE) [![GitHub Issues](https://img.shields.io/github/issues/wecode-ai/Wegent)](https://github.com/wecode-ai/Wegent/issues) Wegent brings team members, AI agents, and personal stand-ins together around the same Issue: describe a goal, assign work, execute tasks, and deliver results. Discussions, execution records, and deliverables stay connected. Work on a local coding project on your own, or hand work across your team in a shared project space. [Download the latest Wegent Desktop](https://github.com/wecode-ai/Wegent/releases/latest) · [Quick start](#quick-start) · [Documentation](https://wecode-ai.github.io/wegent-docs/) · [Contributing](CONTRIBUTING.md) ## One Issue, the whole team [![Watch the 90-second collaboration demo (English)](https://github.com/wecode-ai/Wegent/releases/download/readme-assets/wegent-ai-collaboration-en-20261109.jpg)](https://github.com/wecode-ai/Wegent/releases/download/readme-assets/wegent-ai-collaboration-en-20261109.mp4) [Watch the full demo (90 seconds, English)](https://github.com/wecode-ai/Wegent/releases/download/readme-assets/wegent-ai-collaboration-en-20261109.mp4) Start with “Build an interactive three-column iteration board.” Here is how the work can move forward: 1. **Describe the goal** — Create an Issue and choose a team member, agent, or collaboration group to handle it. 2. **Assign the work** — A configured AI lead can delegate planning and implementation to the appropriate roles. Members receive notifications and open the same Issue. 3. **Execute and deliver** — Members create linked tasks in Wework, use AI to work with files, commands, and tests, then select results to deliver back to the Issue. 4. **Discuss and hand off** — Add feedback and reassign from the discussion. The next member or agent continues with the existing plan and files. 5. **Let a stand-in help, then confirm** — A configured personal stand-in handles work according to its intake scope and processing policy, then hands it back for your confirmation. **Assignment is not completion, and AI output is not personal confirmation.** The Issue connects ownership, execution, discussion, and deliverables so the team can inspect progress, ask questions, and continue the work.

Organize work in a project space with task boards, shared files, and execution status.

## Core capabilities - **People and AI working together** — Assign, discuss, and hand off Issues among team members, agents, and collaboration groups in one project. - **Task execution and delivery** — Create linked tasks from Issues, inspect execution, and deliver selected files and notes back to the project. - **Personal stand-ins (Beta)** — Receive work from authorized project sources according to configured responsibilities and processing policies, with execution records and human-intervention controls. - **Project management and automation** — Organize projects with task boards, shared files, execution records, and deliverables. Configure automatic processing rules and execution queues. - **Local coding workbench** — Use Codex directly with project code, files, commands, and development environments. Review tool activity, tests, and diffs together. - **Reusable agents and execution targets** — Combine models, prompts, Skills, knowledge, and tools. Run tasks locally, on remote work machines, or with server-managed executors. - **Self-hosting** — Deploy Wegent Web and Backend so your team can manage access, permissions, models, scheduling, knowledge services, and remote devices. Personal stand-ins require source authorization, model configuration, and an available execution device. Automatic processing follows project permissions and operation approvals; it does not mean work continues on a powered-off computer. See the [project lead guide](docs/en/wework/personal-stand-in.md#project-lead-controls) for AI lead conversation and automatic-processing requirements; lead conversations currently require experimental features to be enabled. See [Personal stand-in and scenario roles](docs/en/wework/personal-stand-in.md) for configuration. ## Quick start ### Personal use: complete a task in a local project 1. [Download the latest Wegent Desktop installer](https://github.com/wecode-ai/Wegent/releases/latest) and install it. 2. Open the app, follow model setup, and add or select a local project. Local work does not require Wegent Backend login. 3. Create a task describing what to analyze, change, or verify. 4. Inspect agent activity, command output, test results, and file diffs to review the outcome. ### Team collaboration: start with one Issue 1. Create a collaboration project. For shared team access, connect to Wegent Backend and create or join a cloud collaboration project. 2. Add project members. For AI execution, explicitly add agents and configure an available execution environment and model. 3. Create an Issue, describe its goal, and assign it to a member, agent, or collaboration group. 4. Create a linked task from the Issue and deliver the results after execution. Use comments to give feedback and hand work to the next owner. 5. To let a personal stand-in help, configure its project sources, responsibilities, and processing policy in **My stand-in**, then handle human questions and confirmations as needed. New projects do not automatically add agents or enable stand-ins. See [Creating Issues in Collaboration](docs/en/wegent/user-guide/coding/collaboration-issue-home.md) and the [personal stand-in guide](docs/en/wework/personal-stand-in.md) for detailed controls. ### Self-host Wegent Web and Backend To start the self-hosted web application and Backend in standalone mode with Docker: ```bash curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/wecode-ai/Wegent/main/install.sh | bash -s -- --standalone ``` Open http://localhost:3000 and follow the setup flow to create the administrator password and configure a model. See the [Installation Guide](docs/en/wegent/getting-started/installation.md) and [Standalone Mode](docs/en/wegent/deployment/standalone-mode.md) for other deployment options. ## Products ### Wework / Wegent Desktop Wework is the Wegent desktop workbench, connecting project collaboration to execution. It retains the full local coding workflow: organize conversations by project and task, work directly with files, run commands and tests, and review changes and diffs in one workbench. Connect to Backend to use shared project spaces, cloud models, and remote execution devices.

Running and reviewing a local coding task in Wegent Desktop.

### Wegent Web and Backend Wegent Web provides browser-based project collaboration, remote agents, knowledge, automation, and administration. Agents use configured models, knowledge, Skills, and tools. Backend provides shared project resources, access permissions, APIs, scheduling, and execution-device management. Teams can self-host Web and Backend to manage their services and data.

A Wegent remote agent uses tools to generate a Gantt chart.

# Wegent > An open-source work system where people and AI move projects forward together. English | [简体中文](README_zh.md) [![CI](https://github.com/wecode-ai/Wegent/actions/workflows/test.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/wecode-ai/Wegent/actions/workflows/test.yml) [![License](https://img.shields.io/github/license/wecode-ai/Wegent)](LICENSE) [![GitHub Issues](https://img.shields.io/github/issues/wecode-ai/Wegent)](https://github.com/wecode-ai/Wegent/issues) Wegent brings team members, AI agents, and personal stand-ins together around the same Issue: describe a goal, assign work, execute tasks, and deliver results. Discussions, execution records, and deliverables stay connected. Work on a local coding project on your own, or hand work across your team in a shared project space. [Download the latest Wegent Desktop](https://github.com/wecode-ai/Wegent/releases/latest) · [Quick start](#quick-start) · [Documentation](https://wecode-ai.github.io/wegent-docs/) · [Contributing](CONTRIBUTING.md) ## One Issue, the whole team [![Watch the 90-second collaboration demo (English)](https://github.com/wecode-ai/Wegent/releases/download/readme-assets/wegent-ai-collaboration-en-20261109.jpg)](https://github.com/wecode-ai/Wegent/releases/download/readme-assets/wegent-ai-collaboration-en-20261109.mp4) [Watch the full demo (90 seconds, English)](https://github.com/wecode-ai/Wegent/releases/download/readme-assets/wegent-ai-collaboration-en-20261109.mp4) Start with “Build an interactive three-column iteration board.” Here is how the work can move forward: 1. **Describe the goal** — Create an Issue and choose a team member, agent, or collaboration group to handle it. 2. **Assign the work** — A configured AI lead can delegate planning and implementation to the appropriate roles. Members receive notifications and open the same Issue. 3. **Execute and deliver** — Members create linked tasks in Wework, use AI to work with files, commands, and tests, then select results to deliver back to the Issue. 4. **Discuss and hand off** — Add feedback and reassign from the discussion. The next member or agent continues with the existing plan and files. 5. **Let a stand-in help, then confirm** — A configured personal stand-in handles work according to its intake scope and processing policy, then hands it back for your confirmation. **Assignment is not completion, and AI output is not personal confirmation.** The Issue connects ownership, execution, discussion, and deliverables so the team can inspect progress, ask questions, and continue the work.

Organize work in a project space with task boards, shared files, and execution status.

## Core capabilities - **People and AI working together** — Assign, discuss, and hand off Issues among team members, agents, and collaboration groups in one project. - **Task execution and delivery** — Create linked tasks from Issues, inspect execution, and deliver selected files and notes back to the project. - **Personal stand-ins (Beta)** — Receive work from authorized project sources according to configured responsibilities and processing policies, with execution records and human-intervention controls. - **Project management and automation** — Organize projects with task boards, shared files, execution records, and deliverables. Configure automatic processing rules and execution queues. - **Local coding workbench** — Use Codex directly with project code, files, commands, and development environments. Review tool activity, tests, and diffs together. - **Reusable agents and execution targets** — Combine models, prompts, Skills, knowledge, and tools. Run tasks locally, on remote work machines, or with server-managed executors. - **Self-hosting** — Deploy Wegent Web and Backend so your team can manage access, permissions, models, scheduling, knowledge services, and remote devices. Personal stand-ins require source authorization, model configuration, and an available execution device. Automatic processing follows project permissions and operation approvals; it does not mean work continues on a powered-off computer. See the [project lead guide](docs/en/wework/personal-stand-in.md#project-lead-controls) for AI lead conversation and automatic-processing requirements; lead conversations currently require experimental features to be enabled. See [Personal stand-in and scenario roles](docs/en/wework/personal-stand-in.md) for configuration. ## Quick start ### Personal use: complete a task in a local project 1. [Download the latest Wegent Desktop installer](https://github.com/wecode-ai/Wegent/releases/latest) and install it. 2. Open the app, follow model setup, and add or select a local project. Local work does not require Wegent Backend login. 3. Create a task describing what to analyze, change, or verify. 4. Inspect agent activity, command output, test results, and file diffs to review the outcome. ### Team collaboration: start with one Issue 1. Create a collaboration project. For shared team access, connect to Wegent Backend and create or join a cloud collaboration project. 2. Add project members. For AI execution, explicitly add agents and configure an available execution environment and model. 3. Create an Issue, describe its goal, and assign it to a member, agent, or collaboration group. 4. Create a linked task from the Issue and deliver the results after execution. Use comments to give feedback and hand work to the next owner. 5. To let a personal stand-in help, configure its project sources, responsibilities, and processing policy in **My stand-in**, then handle human questions and confirmations as needed. New projects do not automatically add agents or enable stand-ins. See [Creating Issues in Collaboration](docs/en/wegent/user-guide/coding/collaboration-issue-home.md) and the [personal stand-in guide](docs/en/wework/personal-stand-in.md) for detailed controls. ### Self-host Wegent Web and Backend To start the self-hosted web application and Backend in standalone mode with Docker: ```bash curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/wecode-ai/Wegent/main/install.sh | bash -s -- --standalone ``` Open http://localhost:3000 and follow the setup flow to create the administrator password and configure a model. See the [Installation Guide](docs/en/wegent/getting-started/installation.md) and [Standalone Mode](docs/en/wegent/deployment/standalone-mode.md) for other deployment options. ## Products ### Wework / Wegent Desktop Wework is the Wegent desktop workbench, connecting project collaboration to execution. It retains the full local coding workflow: organize conversations by project and task, work directly with files, run commands and tests, and review changes and diffs in one workbench. Connect to Backend to use shared project spaces, cloud models, and remote execution devices.

Running and reviewing a local coding task in Wegent Desktop.

### Wegent Web and Backend Wegent Web provides browser-based project collaboration, remote agents, knowledge, automation, and administration. Agents use configured models, knowledge, Skills, and tools. Backend provides shared project resources, access permissions, APIs, scheduling, and execution-device management. Teams can self-host Web and Backend to manage their services and data.

A Wegent remote agent uses tools to generate a Gantt chart.

## Development Requires Node.js 22.15+ (22.x) or 23.8+ (Node.js 24 recommended), and pnpm: ```bash pnpm install pnpm --filter wework dev ``` To run the macOS desktop app: ```bash pnpm --filter wework dev:mac ``` See [wework/README.md](wework/README.md) for desktop development, build, and release instructions. `wework/` is the current desktop application source directory. In the desktop architecture, Electron provides system capabilities and process management, DeepSeek Harness (DSH) hosts the product UI and plugins, and Executor manages tasks and sessions while driving Codex execution. See the [DSH application host](wework/dsh/app-wework/README.en.md) for plugin extension points and [Cloud project collaboration architecture](docs/en/wegent/developer-guide/cloud-project-collaboration.md) for shared-resource and execution boundaries. ## Repository map ### Products and services | Directory | Responsibility | | -------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------- | | `wework/` | Wegent Desktop (Electron, Vite, React) | | `wework-mobile/` | Independent Expo application for iOS and Android | | `frontend/` | Wegent Web (Next.js, React) | | `backend/` | Default public API, business logic, and data models | | `backend-rs/` | Rust hybrid gateway and APIs that have completed migration | | `executor/` | Rust task executor, local-device runtime, and Codex integration | | `executor_manager/` | Server-side executor scheduling, sandboxes, and orchestration | | `chat_shell/` | Lightweight chat and agent runtime | | `knowledge_runtime/` | Knowledge indexing and retrieval API | | `knowledge_doc_converter/` | Document parsing and asynchronous conversion service | ### Shared code and developer tools | Directory | Responsibility | | ------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | `knowledge_engine/` | Reusable Python kernel for parsing, indexing, vector stores, and retrieval | | `shared/` | Python models, protocols, utilities, and telemetry shared by services | | `packages/` | TypeScript chat and collaboration modules shared by Web and Desktop | | `sdk/` | Plugin authentication, build, creation, and DingTalk workspace SDKs | | `wegent-cli/` | Python CLI for managing Wegent CRD resources | ### Infrastructure, tests, and documentation | Directory | Responsibility | | ----------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | `docker/` | Service images, standalone resources, and the `docker/telemetry/` observability stack | | `scripts/` | Installation, release, acceptance, repository-policy, and development automation | | `tests/` | Cross-service Playwright integration tests and installation tests | | `docs/` | English and Chinese user docs, developer docs, architecture, and historical designs | | `patches/` | Third-party dependency patches used by pnpm `patchedDependencies` | | `LICENSES/` | Third-party license texts required for repository distribution | | `.github/` | CI, release workflows, composite actions, and repository automation | ### Root entry points | File | Responsibility | | -------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------- | | `start.sh`, `install.sh` | Local startup and self-hosted installation | | `build_image.sh`, `build_image_mac.sh` | Multi-architecture and host Docker image builds | | `docker-compose*.yml` | Default, build, and E2E Compose orchestration | | `package.json`, `pnpm-workspace.yaml` | JavaScript/TypeScript workspace definition | | `pyproject.toml`, `uv.lock` | Repository-level Python tooling and lock metadata | | `AGENTS.md`, `CLAUDE.md` | Contributor rules and compatibility symlink | ## Documentation - [Wegent Desktop documentation](docs/en/wework/README.md) - [Desktop development and release](wework/README.md) - [Wegent quick start](docs/en/wegent/getting-started/quick-start.md) - [Installation and deployment](docs/en/wegent/getting-started/installation.md) - [Core concepts](docs/en/wegent/concepts/core-concepts.md) - [Developer guide](docs/en/wegent/developer-guide/README.md) - [Troubleshooting](docs/en/wegent/troubleshooting.md) ## Contributing Bug reports, documentation improvements, code contributions, and new ways of using Wegent are all welcome. - [Contributing Guide](CONTRIBUTING.md) - [Security Policy](SECURITY.md) - [GitHub Issues](https://github.com/wecode-ai/Wegent/issues) - DingTalk Community: “wework社区交流”, group ID `190890002451` - [Discord Community](https://discord.gg/MVzJzyqEUp) - [License](LICENSE) ## Contributors Thanks to everyone who helps Wegent grow.

See [Creating Issues in Collaboration](docs/en/wegent/user-guide/coding/collaboration-issue-home.md) and the [personal stand-in guide](docs/en/wework/personal-stand-in.md) for detailed controls. ### Self-host Wegent Web and Backend To start the self-hosted web application and Backend in standalone mode with Docker: ```bash curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/wecode-ai/Wegent/main/install.sh | bash -s -- --standalone ``` Open http://localhost:3000 and follow the setup flow to create the administrator password and configure a model. See the [Installation Guide](docs/en/wegent/getting-started/installation.md) and [Standalone Mode](docs/en/wegent/deployment/standalone-mode.md) for other deployment options. ## Products ### Wework / Wegent Desktop Wework is the Wegent desktop workbench, connecting project collaboration to execution. It retains the full local coding workflow: organize conversations by project and task, work directly with files, run commands and tests, and review changes and diffs in one workbench. Connect to Backend to use shared project spaces, cloud models, and remote execution devices.

Running and reviewing a local coding task in Wegent Desktop.

### Wegent Web and Backend Wegent Web provides browser-based project collaboration, remote agents, knowledge, automation, and administration. Agents use configured models, knowledge, Skills, and tools. Backend provides shared project resources, access permissions, APIs, scheduling, and execution-device management. Teams can self-host Web and Backend to manage their services and data.

A Wegent remote agent uses tools to generate a Gantt chart.

evidence.readmeExcerpt:
# dsh-aiignore — context noise guard for DeepSeek Harness

A Host plugin that checks a workspace **when a session opens it** and tells the
agent which files would waste its context — build output, lockfiles, logs,
huge files.

The scan is the same one the [`ai-context-doctor`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/ai-context-doctor)
CLI runs; this package only decides *when* to run it and how to phrase the
result for the model. Everything is local: no network, no API key, no upload.

## Requirements

| | |
| --- | --- |
| DeepSeek Harness | `>= 0.2.0` — the version that ships `sidebarRightTabs`; declared as `engines.dsh` in `package.json` and in every market-index entry, so an older Harness refuses the install instead of half-loading it |
| Node.js | `>= 18` — the Host half uses `node:test` and `structuredClone` |
| Permissions | none. No network, no API key, no telemetry; it reads the workspace and writes `.aiignore` and `.aiignore.policy.json` |

Without a sidebar service the same button opens the panel as a floating card,
so an older or trimmed-down Harness still gets the report, just not the tab.

## What the agent sees

When a workspace scores below the threshold, the agent receives one short note
before it starts reading files:

```text
[ai-context-doctor] This workspace scores 29/100 for context health: 71% of 1.7 MB in 24 files is likely noise.
Biggest offenders: dist/ (400.0 KB, generated build output), package-lock.json (400.0 KB, lockfile).
Suggested .aiignore: dist/, package-lock.json, *.log.
Do not read those files unless the task needs them; ask before opening large generated files.
```

Clean workspaces get no message at all — a plugin that speaks on every session
becomes noise itself.

## The panel

The bundle also ships a browser half. A folder button sits beside the add-files
button in the composer; clicking it opens the **right sidebar** on the
**AIignore** tab, and expands the sidebar if it was collapsed. On a Host without
sidebar services the same button opens the panel as a floating card instead, so
one plugin covers both.

![The Protection tab, light theme](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/WJDdidi-1/ai-context-doctor/main/docs/assets/panel-protection-light.png)

![The Files tab: what this session read and wrote](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/WJDdidi-1/ai-context-doctor/main/docs/assets/panel-files-light.png)

Three tabs inside, and the first one exists to answer a single question: *is
this doing anything?*

- **Protection** — a score, one button, and nothing else competing with them.
  The number is **this conversation's current score**: the one it would have if
  the rules in force applied to what it actually read. There is no *before →
  after* pair to read — one number, and it moves when the rules or the strength
  move, because it is computed from them. (The folder's own score, rules and
  all, lives on **Settings** as `On disk 22 · Reaches the model 71`, where the
  arithmetic belongs.) A folder nobody has scanned says *not scanned yet*
  rather than printing a dash under a label that promises a number, and a
  conversation that read nothing junk-worthy says so in words instead of a
  zero. **Optimize now** is always there — it
  rescans, writes whatever is missing, re-scores, and reports what moved, so
  the interaction is: look, press, watch the number change.
  The **strength ladder** is one click away in *Fine-tune the strength*: five
  notches, each labelled with the score this folder would have there, because
  five scores at once answer a question nobody asked yet. Picking a notch
  writes it, rescans and repaints from the new report. Below that, **one notch
  stricter** with the number attached ("would block 2 more files, about
  65k–81k tokens"), then the files actually kept out and how many rules are in
  force.
- **Files** — opens on **the files this session touched** (what the agent read
  and what it wrote), then lets you browse the whole workspace a directory at a
  time. Search, filter by verdict — and when a filter has nothing in it, the
  panel says which filter that was instead of looking empty. The three verdicts
  are spelled out right under the filters: `noise` is regenerated by a build, a
  lockfile or a log; `review` is worth a look before it goes in (env files,
  deploy scripts, big data); `ignored` already has a line in `.aiignore`. Under
  that, **Worth a rule** lists what the scanner would still add (`+ *.log`,
  `+ coverage/`) — one click writes the line and rescans. A noise file's detail
  card offers the widest rule that covers it, `Add dist/`, not only its own
  path, because a per-file line is a rule you write again every build.
- **Settings** — everything you can change, off the screen that answers *is it
  working*: **Rules in .aiignore** with an × per line, the note for the agent
  with a preview of exactly the text it will read, and the five-dimension
  arithmetic folded away at the bottom. It points at Protection for the
  strength ladder instead of keeping a second copy of it — two controls for one
  setting drift, and the copy that stops being authoritative is always the one
  on the page nobody is looking at.

  It no longer asks you to imagine what the note does: three one-click
  sentences, then a preview of **exactly the text the agent will read** before
  your next message.

- **One button runs the job.** *Optimize now* reads the folder, writes the
  rules, re-scores and moves the number on screen. While it runs you see the two
  steps it actually performs, each marked done only when its work is finished —
  no percentage bar inventing progress the Host never reported.
- **The rules are visible, and removable one at a time.** Under the score sits
  **Rules in .aiignore**: every line that is in force, each with an ×. Removing
  one edits exactly that line — comments and the other rules stay — so a rule
  you disagree with is one click away instead of an all-or-nothing undo.
- **The strength is part of the score, not a separate page.** Five buttons from
  *Off* to *Strict*, each already scored against your workspace before you commit
  to one, so the difference between *Balanced* and *Strict* is a number you read
  instead of a slider you drag. There is no slider any more: two ways to say the
  same thing was one too many. Each notch says what it stops and what that costs;
  the Host stores it in `.aiignore.policy.json`; the read guard and the scan share
  the same predicate, so saving a notch re-scans and the number moves.

### The words this panel uses

Five terms carry most of the panel, and they are used the same way everywhere —
in the tabs, the tooltips, the changelog and this file.

| Term | Means | Not to be confused with |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **held back** | a read your rules stopped, or would stop. The counter, the list under it and the badge all say this. | *refused* — the guard turning a read away right now | 
| **rule** | one line in `.aiignore`, matched against paths | a *note*, which is text for the agent, not a rule |
| **notch** | one of the five strength settings, from Off to Strict | the *score*, which the notch changes |
| **score** | two numbers: this conversation, and what still reaches the model | *tokens*, which are a byte-based estimate |
| **noise** | build output, lockfiles, logs, generated files and anything over 1 MB | *review*, which means look before you decide |

### Following the conversation, not a folder

The panel asks the Host who the current conversation is, and the Host reads the
session store: `<DSH_HOME>/sessions/*/session-*/session.v4.jsonl.zstd` is an
append-only zstd file whose **first frame is a JSON header** carrying the
session id and its `cwd`. The most recently written log is the conversation in
front of you, and its header names the folder — no guessing from directory
names, and no dependency on the workspace index ever having been told about that
session. The header names the workspace; the guard, the score and the file list
then all speak about that one folder.

The Chat tab's picker shows the conversations this app knows about, newest
first, with `current` on the live one. Picking an older one re-reads *that*
conversation — header title, turn count and file list all switch — and a
`showing an earlier conversation` chip appears in the header; clicking it takes
you back to the live one.

The folder button keeps a menu: **follow this conversation** (the default),
**pick another folder…**, or **stop pinning** — so a choice made once is a choice
you can take back. Every workspace this app has been used in is also listed on
the **Context across your workspaces** page in the left rail, scored with the
same rules.

### One click, with a way back

**Optimize this workspace** appends the scanner's suggestion to `.aiignore`,
keeping the lines already there, then reports the score before and after. The
previous file is held in memory for the session, so **Undo** puts it back byte
for byte — and if optimize created the file, undo removes it.

Two decisions per file, available from the tree, the session list and the report:

- **Read once** (the report calls it **Read it anyway**) pre-approves a path for
  the rest of the Host run, including one the session has not tried yet.
  Reloading the Harness forgets it — a temporary override should stay temporary.
- **Never read it** appends the path to the workspace's `.aiignore`. That is the
  durable direction, because the file is the record: it survives restarts, shows
  up in review, and you can delete the line yourself.

One workspace can hold many conversations, so the panel never averages them:
the **Chat** tab's picker lists the conversations this app knows, marks the one
currently open, and every number above it is that conversation's. There is no
separate "follow" entry in the picker — the folder button already means
follow, and two controls for one state is one control too many. When the session
store cannot answer, the panel falls back to the directory the slot hands it
(`?cwd=`), then to the agent and session registries, then to whatever was
scanned last. Only an absolute path to an existing directory is accepted.

The aggregate view lives in the left rail, under New Session: **AIignore** lists
every conversation this app has run, worst first, and can act without opening
any of them. Each row shows the conversation's title, folder, turns, files read
and size; the score on the left is the one your rules and strength leave behind,
with the pre-rule number trailing behind it when the two differ, and a
`N kept out` badge once a clean-up covers something. **Scan again** refreshes,
**Clean up N** writes that conversation's suggestions, **Open the panel** jumps
to it. It is served by `GET /aiignore/conversations` (twenty-one routes in total).

Both numbers are computed from the session projection, never from a guess: the
conversation score is what that chat was actually handed, and the effective
score re-runs the same decision the guard uses — rules, then strength — so a
conversation that read `dist/` before you had a rule shows `74` and `100`
afterwards, with the file named under **No longer reaching the model**.

Styling comes from the Host's design tokens (`--dsw-*`) with fallbacks, so the
panel follows light and dark themes instead of shipping its own palette. Every
control is reachable with `Tab`.

Loading, empty and failure are three states of one component, on all three
surfaces that fetch anything (the panel, the left page, the strength table): a
skeleton while a request is in flight, one sentence when there is nothing to
show, and an error that names what failed, carries the real status
(`status 500`), and offers a retry that repeats the same request. Nothing
silently disappears — the strength table used to vanish while it loaded — and
nothing invents a cause: an unreachable server says `network`, a rejected one
says the status.

The panel talks to the Host half over twenty-one same-origin routes
(`GET /aiignore/report`, `GET /aiignore/tree?dir=`, `GET /aiignore/overview`,
`GET /aiignore/sessions`, `GET /aiignore/workspaces`, `GET /aiignore/levels`,
`GET /aiignore/debug`,
`GET/POST /aiignore/notes`, `GET/POST /aiignore/policy`,
`GET /aiignore/upload?digest=`, `POST /aiignore/scan`,
`POST /aiignore/client-report`, `POST /aiignore/optimize`,
`POST /aiignore/optimize/undo`, `POST /aiignore/allow`,
`POST /aiignore/ignore`, `POST /aiignore/unignore`,
`POST /aiignore/rules`, `POST /aiignore/rules/delete`). The upload route serves a thumbnail and refuses
anything that is not a 64-hex digest inside the attachment store; the unignore
route removes the rule that names a file and refuses symlinks and directories,
while `rules/delete` removes one rule line by its exact text (`dist/`, `*.log`)
and never touches a comment, while `rules` writes one rule that was suggested
without a file to name (`*.log`) — it checks the shape (relative, no `..`, no
leading `/`) and clears the scan caches so the next read sees it. They
answer for the most recently scanned workspace and set `no-store`; the only one
that returns file bytes is the upload thumbnail, and it only ever returns an
image the user already handed to this session. The Host half installs them through `ctx.inject(['webServer'])`,
so a profile without a web server still gets the read guard — it just has no panel.
There is no authentication beyond a same-origin check: like every
`ctx.webServer` route, this one inherits the loopback bind of the Harness and
must not be exposed to a network.

![The Protection tab, dark theme](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/WJDdidi-1/ai-context-doctor/main/docs/assets/panel-protection-dark.png)

![Settings, dark theme: rules and the note for the agent](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/WJDdidi-1/ai-context-doctor/main/docs/assets/panel-settings-dark.png)

### When something looks wrong

Settings ends with a **Diagnostics** fold: plugin version, Node, platform, data
folder, workspace, how many conversations it can see, how many rules are in
effect, and which surface (sidebar tab or floating card) you got. One button
copies it as plain text.

It is built to be pasted in public — the home directory is shortened to `~` and
there is no token, session id or conversation title anywhere in it.

### Looking at the panel without a Harness

`dev/preview.html` renders the real panel against the Host's real design tokens
with mock data: both themes, four scenarios (noisy, healthy, freshly opened,
request failing), and `?nosidebar=1` to see the floating-card fallback. Open the
file in a browser; no build, no server. It is a development page and is not part
of the published package.

### Behaviour tests

`test/interaction.test.mjs` mounts the real `client.js` in Node — jsdom, the real
React, a host context that records what the bundle registers, and stubbed
`/aiignore/*` routes — and then does what a person does:

```js
const panel = await mountClient({ file: 'client.js', fetch: createFetch(routes) });
await panel.press('#aicd-tab-protect', 'ArrowRight');   // the tab moves
await panel.click('[data-aicd-menu-btn]');               // the menu opens
await panel.press('[role="menu"]', 'Escape');            // and closes on Escape
await panel.click('[data-wide="true"]');                 // Optimize posts once
assert.match(panel.text(), /96/);                        // and the score moves
```

The tool is [`dsh-plugin-toolkit/testkit`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/dsh-plugin-toolkit).
The older `*.test.mjs` guards that read this file as text are still here: they
are fast and they catch a deleted string, but they could never have caught the
bug where Optimize was hidden — only mounting it could.

### Visual baselines

`docs/assets/baseline/` holds the eight screenshots the panel is measured
against: four preview scenarios (*noisy*, *healthy*, *fresh*, *broken*) in both
themes, cropped to the 420 × 660 the sidebar actually gives it. They are
committed, not generated in CI — this repository has no headless browser.

After an **intentional** visual change, re-capture all eight. Each one is a
cold load of its own URL, which the manifest records per file:

```
dev/preview.html?scenario=noisy&theme=light
dev/preview.html?scenario=noisy&theme=dark
...  (healthy, fresh, broken × light, dark)
```

Open each URL at 1280 × 800, crop to the panel, and rewrite
`docs/assets/baseline/manifest.json` with each file's size, SHA-256 and URL.
The URL is not decoration: three baselines once drifted because they had been
taken with `?first=1` and `?failreport=1` and nothing recorded it, so the
difference looked like a rendering bug. Then run:

```
node plugin/scripts/check-baseline.mjs
```

It fails when a baseline is missing, edited by hand, or left out of the
manifest — the change that looks like a small fix but moves everything.

The crop is fixed so the images stay comparable: with the preview open at
1280 × 800, the panel occupies `(861, 100)` to `(1281, 760)` — the preview's own
toolbar sits above it, and a crop that included it would compare the harness.

## Install

Through the Plugin Manager:

- **From npm** — install `dsh-aiignore`.
- **From a checkout** — install the `plugin/` directory of this repository.

Installing a local directory links it, so re-check the files directly: `files`
does not filter a linked directory.

### From the plugin market

Harness has no central store: the **Discover** tab lists whatever indexes the
user adds. This repository publishes one at

```text
https://raw.githubusercontent.com/WJDdidi-1/ai-context-doctor/main/market/index.json
```

To use it:

1. Open **Plugins** in the Web sidebar.
2. Beside **Experimental plugins**, open **More** and switch on **Custom plugin
   markets**. The Plugins page then gains an **Installed** / **Discover** split.
3. In **Discover**, add the index URL above.
4. Install **dsh-aiignore** from the result.

The Harness checks the declared `engines.dsh` range before installing and
refuses the plugin if the running version falls outside it.

## Configure

Values go in the plugin's `config` row in `cordis.patch.yml`:

```yaml
- insert:
    - id: ai-context-doctor
      name: 'dsh-aiignore'
      config:
        healthThreshold: 80
        maxFiles: 20000
        maxBytes: 268435456
```

| key | default | meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `healthThreshold` | `80` | Inject only when the workspace scores below this. `100` disables the notice without uninstalling. |
| `maxFiles` | `20000` | Stop scanning after this many files. |
| `maxBytes` | `268435456` | Stop scanning after this many bytes (256 MiB). |
| `readPolicy` | `deny` | `deny` refuses `read` calls on the noisy files below; `off` only warns at session start. |

The caps exist because the scan is a synchronous directory walk: without them,
opening a huge monorepo would stall the Host.

The guard also refuses anything the workspace's own `.aiignore` lists, including
files the size heuristic considers clean. A hand-written rule beats the
heuristic, and editing the file takes effect on the next read.

## What it refuses to read

With `readPolicy: deny`, the plugin installs a tool guard that refuses `read`
calls on the same files the notice names:

| refused | why |
| --- | --- |
| `dist/`, `build/`, `coverage/`, `.next/`, `.turbo/` | generated output; the source is what matters |
| `package-lock.json`, `pnpm-lock.yaml`, `yarn.lock` | thousands of lines of resolved versions |
| `*.log` | local run output, usually stale |
| files over 1 MiB | a single read can consume the whole budget |

The refusal is a message, not a silent failure: it names the file, its size and
the tokens the read would have cost, so the agent can tell the user instead of
retrying. Templates like `.env.example` and scripts with `deploy` in the path
are **never** blocked — they are small, and a wrong guess there loses real
information.

Every refusal is recorded per workspace (`getSkippedReads`) so the UI half can
list what this session did not open.

## Limits

- The notice fires once per workspace per Host run; changing the directory in a
  session does not re-trigger it.
- The score is a size heuristic; token figures are a range from the measured
  3.08–4.32 bytes-per-token ratio, not an exact count.
- `bash`, `grep` and other tools that can read a file indirectly are not
  intercepted: the guard only sees the `read` tool.
- `.gitignore` is ignored on purpose: the point is what the agent *would* read,
  not what git tracks.
- The panel follows the conversation whose log was written last. Switching to a
  conversation you have not touched since this Host run started moves it only
  after that conversation writes something, so it can lag one click behind.
- Switching the interface language takes effect the next time the panel opens;
  the open panel does not re-render.

`ai-context-doctor` from the same repository.

# AI Context Doctor

[![npm](https://img.shields.io/npm/v/ai-context-doctor)](https://www.npmjs.com/package/ai-context-doctor)
[![CI](https://github.com/WJDdidi-1/ai-context-doctor/actions/workflows/ci.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/WJDdidi-1/ai-context-doctor/actions/workflows/ci.yml)
[![license](https://img.shields.io/npm/l/ai-context-doctor)](https://github.com/WJDdidi-1/ai-context-doctor/blob/main/LICENSE)
[![downloads](https://img.shields.io/npm/dm/ai-context-doctor)](https://www.npmjs.com/package/ai-context-doctor)

[中文说明](https://github.com/WJDdidi-1/ai-context-doctor/blob/main/docs/README.zh-CN.md)

**AI coding agents read your repository file by file. Some of those files are garbage — build output, logs, lockfiles, a 40 MB data dump. This tool finds them in a few seconds and tells you what to keep away from the agent.**

```bash
npx ai-context-doctor
```

No install, no login, no API key, nothing uploaded. It only reads file names, sizes, and your ignore/policy files.

## What it looks like

Real output of `node bin/ai-context-doctor.js ./demo-ai-context-noise-repo`, run from a clean checkout of this repository:

```text
AI Context Doctor

Repo: demo-ai-context-noise-repo
Scanned: 8 files, 1.50 MB

AI Context Health: 43/100
Status: Too much noise for an AI coding agent

What reaches the model: 78/100
  strength 3 (Balanced) · 335.0 KB of 1.50 MB let through

Blocked from the model:
- coverage/lcov.info           16.7 KB   build · category rule at strength 3 (Balanced)
- data/export.json             1.00 MB   large · file > 1.00 MB at strength 3 (Balanced)
- dist/app.bundle.js          106.9 KB   build · category rule at strength 3 (Balanced)
- logs/dev.log                 18.4 KB   log · category rule at strength 3 (Balanced)
- package-lock.json            35.2 KB   lockfile · category rule at strength 3 (Balanced)

Where the points go:
  context noise          - 21.3 / 30
  context volume         - 16.2 / 25
  one file dominating    -   20 / 20
  file sprawl            -    0 / 15
  binary payloads        -    0 / 10

Context noise estimate:
78% likely noise
22% likely useful source context

Top context waste:
1. data/export.json            1.00 MB   large file
2. dist/                      106.9 KB   generated build output
3. package-lock.json           35.2 KB   lockfile
4. logs/dev.log                18.4 KB   local log file
5. coverage/                   16.7 KB   test coverage output

Review before sharing:
- .env.example             environment template (usually safe to share)
- scripts/deploy.sh        deployment script

Suggested .aiignore:
coverage/
dist/
*.log
package-lock.json

At strength 3 the strength already blocks these, so they change nothing that reaches the model. They bite at a lower strength.

Next step:
Run this before asking your coding agent to inspect a larger repo.
```

## How to read it

| Line | What it means |
| --- | --- |
| `Scanned: 8 files, 1.50 MB` | What was actually walked. `.git/` and `node_modules/` are skipped. |
| `AI Context Health: 43/100` | Five separate losses, subtracted from 100: noise (30), sheer size (25), one file dominating (20), file count (15), binaries (10). The first is what rules can move; the other four describe the folder itself, so a clean but enormous repository no longer scores 100. |
| `What reaches the model` | The same score after `.aiignore` rules and the chosen strength are applied, plus how many bytes they let through. |
| `Blocked from the model` | Up to five blocked files, each with its category and the rule or strength cutoff that decided it. |
| `Where the points go` | The five losses behind the health score, so a low number is explainable instead of mysterious. |
| `Status:` | Just the score in words: 85+ clean, 60–84 some noise, below 60 too much. |
| `Top context waste` | The five biggest offenders with the reason each was flagged. |
| `Review before sharing` | Files that look like credentials or deploy scripts. **The tool does not claim they are secret** — it says look before you paste the repo into a chat. |
| `Suggested .aiignore` | Lines you can paste into an ignore file. Nothing is written for you. |

## How it decides

![How a repository and a conversation are scored](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/WJDdidi-1/ai-context-doctor/main/docs/assets/architecture.svg)

Two paths read the same decision function, which is why the number on the panel and the files the agent was actually kept from cannot disagree: the scan turns a folder into files, bytes and noise and scores it, and every read the agent makes is checked against the same `.aiignore` rules at the chosen strength. Optimize writes those rules, and the next scan and the next read both pick them up.

## What you can do with it

- **Before you hand a repo to an agent** — run it, then `--write` the suggested lines into `.aiignore` instead of copying them by hand.
- **On a repo you just cloned** — see how much of it is generated output before the agent drowns in it.
- **In CI** — `--json` gives a versioned object (`schemaVersion: 1`), so you can pin the shape and fail a build when context health drops.
- **In your own tool** — `require('ai-context-doctor')` exposes the same scan as a function.
- **Inside DeepSeek Harness** — install [`dsh-aiignore`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/dsh-aiignore) and the agent is told automatically when a session opens a noisy workspace, so you do not have to remember to run anything.

## Install

Run it without installing anything:

```bash
npx ai-context-doctor
```

Or install it once:

```bash
npm install -g ai-context-doctor
```

Requires Node.js 18 or newer.

## Usage

```bash
ai-context-doctor              # scan the current directory
ai-context-doctor ../some-repo # scan another repository
ai-context-doctor --json       # machine-readable output
ai-context-doctor --explain src/index.js   # explain one file's verdict
ai-context-doctor --write      # add the suggested rules to .aiignore
ai-context-doctor --write --dry-run   # show what --write would add
ai-context-doctor --help
ai-context-doctor --version
```

### Why is this file blocked?

From the shipped demo repository:

```bash
node bin/ai-context-doctor.js ./demo-ai-context-noise-repo --explain package-lock.json
```

Prints the verdict for one path, the rule that decided it, the category it
belongs to, and what letting it through would cost:

```text
AI Context Doctor — explain

Path: package-lock.json
Verdict: blocked
Rule: strength 3 (Balanced) skips lockfiles
Category: lockfile
Size: 35.2 KB (~8342–11700 tokens)
Why: lockfile
Score impact: allowing it would cost 4 points (78/100 -> 74/100).
```

If a line in `.aiignore` decided it, the `Rule:` line prints that exact line
instead of a strength. When a `!` line is what kept the path — for example
`*.md` followed by `!README.md` — the line is named too, with
`(re-included)` after it, so the explanation does not claim that no rule
matched. An unblocked path says `Verdict: not blocked`. An unknown path is an
error with exit code 2, not a silent "not blocked". Add `--json` to get the same
explanation as an object; a released path keeps `blocked: false` because it
still reaches the model, while `rule` names the `!` line that kept it.

### Run the example

[`examples/`](https://github.com/WJDdidi-1/ai-context-doctor/blob/main/examples/README.md)
has a self-contained walkthrough of `--explain`. It builds a throwaway
repository, runs the real CLI twice — once with no `.aiignore`, then once after
adding a rule — prints both verdicts, and deletes the fixture:

```bash
node examples/explain-blocked-path.js
# or
npm run example
```

No install or network access; it uses Node.js built-ins and the code in this
checkout. The first verdict is a lockfile blocked by strength 3, the second
names the exact `.aiignore` line.

### Writing `.aiignore`

```bash
npx ai-context-doctor --write
```

`--write` appends the rules the report suggests to `.aiignore` in the scanned
directory. It only appends: comments and rules you already have stay exactly as
they are, and running it twice adds nothing the second time. If the file does
not exist it is created with a two-line header.

`--write --dry-run` prints what would be added and writes nothing.

It will not follow a symbolic link, and it refuses to replace a directory that
happens to be called `.aiignore`.

#### Order and `!`

Rules are applied in file order and the **last matching line decides**, the same
way gitignore works. A leading `!` is an exception: it releases a path that an
earlier line would have blocked.

```text
*.md
!README.md
```

`README.md` reaches the model; every other Markdown file is still blocked by
`*.md`. Order matters: put the negation after the broad rule. If the lines are
reversed, `*.md` matches last and the README is blocked again. A `!` line that
matches nothing changes nothing, and a broad rule below a negation re-blocks
whatever

# dsh-resume

This folder is a frozen snapshot of the files the compatibility sample audits.
Its `engines.dsh` range is the real one from `L3n3L/dsh-resume@0.1.3`:

## Requirements

- DeepSeek Harness `>=0.1.0-rc.6 <0.2.0-0`

```json
"engines": {
  "dsh": ">=0.1.0-rc.6 <0.2.0-0"
}
```

The heading is here on purpose: the sample isolates the host-range verdict, and
the remote audit still checks README requirements. Upstream's localized README
does not use a `## Requirements` heading, so a live audit of the repository can
also add a `readme` failure to the same row.

`node scripts/compatibility-sample.mjs` compares this manifest with the
`0.2.2-alpha.3` canary from the reports. Add `--host <version>` to ask the same
frozen manifest about the DSH version you run; the wrapper then exits with the
replayed CLI's status, so `--host 0.1.5` exits `0` and a range-excluding version
exits `1`.

# dsh-plugin-toolkit

[![npm](https://img.shields.io/npm/v/dsh-plugin-toolkit)](https://www.npmjs.com/package/dsh-plugin-toolkit)
